Community That Survives the Airdrop

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 18 May 2026 · 8-minute read · Growth

Incentives buy activity, not community. Build for the people who stay when the payments stop, give them a job, and keep the record of who they are on channels you own. The on-chain record is consistent: two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed 93% of recipients had sold all their UNI, and an academic study of nine airdrops found up to 66% of tokens were sold soon after claiming.

This is the crypto chapter of our guide to building a community that lasts. It applies the argument that community is a job, not a number to the one sector where the number is easiest to inflate.

Farmers sell, and that is fine

An airdrop farmer is a rational actor doing exactly what the programme paid for. They completed the task, claimed the reward and sold it. Nothing in that sequence was a relationship.

Messias, Yaish and Livshits studied nine airdrops, including Uniswap, Arbitrum and Optimism, using on-chain data to October 2024. For several, a large share of tokens went straight to exchanges as the recipient's first action: 65.75% for Lido, 58.67% for 1inch and 48.21% for Optimism. Within 24 hours, 66.09% of 1inch recipients had sent tokens to an exchange. The authors conclude that airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own".

The Uniswap airdrop of September 2020 is the clearest long view. A Dune analysis two years later found more than 75% of recipients sold within seven days, 93% had sold everything, and about 98% had never taken part in governance.

The mistake is not that farmers exist. The mistake is counting them as users. The claim rate goes in the launch deck, the sell-through is never mentioned, and the team wonders where everyone went. In crypto, the number is unusually easy to inflate. So the job matters more, not less.

Plan it as an acquisition cost

Plan the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected loss rate. Then design for the fraction who stay.

Price outcomes vary with design. Keyrock, a crypto market maker, reviewed 62 airdrops across six chains in 2024 and found only eight were trading above their launch price after 90 days. Larger distributions, above 10% of supply, held up better over time than small ones. Price is not community, but it shapes who has a reason to stay.

Line in the planWhat to write down before launch
Expected sell-throughShare of claimants likely to sell within 30 days
Cost per retained userValue distributed divided by users active after incentives stop
Sybil exclusionRules, tests and appeal route, fixed before the snapshot
Holder jobThe work holders will be invited to do
Owned recordWhere the member list and contribution log live

A token distribution deserves the cost-per-outcome treatment our piece on demand generation economics applies to any acquisition budget.

Quests, points and the platform you do not own

Quest platforms produce completion. A wallet connects, follows an account, retweets a post, joins a server. Every box is ticked and nobody has used the product.

Pay-to-post programmes were the same pattern with more money attached. On 15 January 2026, X's product lead announced that X had revoked API access for apps that paid users to post. The Block reported the KAITO token fell 14.5% that day, and Kaito said it would wind down its incentivised leaderboards. Teams that had built their whole engagement layer on that machinery lost it in one policy change they had no vote on.

The lesson is platform dependency, not any one platform. Any channel you rent can be repriced or removed. Our piece on distribution when the platforms are closed covers this across sectors. In crypto, the dependency is usually deeper and the switch-off is usually faster. Keep using the platforms. Just never let them hold the only copy of your community.

Earned allocation with filters that bite

If you are going to distribute tokens to users, distribute them for behaviour you want repeated. Not for showing up. For using the product in the way a long-term user would.

That means allocation weighted to usage over time, not usage in a single window. Position size matters less than consistency. Sybil filtering is a product feature, built before the snapshot, not a clean-up after. Messias and colleagues document a farmer on ZKsync Era who used more than 20,000 accounts and deployed a fake exchange to qualify for one distribution. Their recommendations include scaling rewards with the costs users incur, and running several smaller distributions over time rather than one.

Expect the filters to be contested. Publish the rules in advance, apply them without exception, and keep an appeals channel that a human reads. The people who argue in good faith are often the users you most want to keep. Our companion piece on airdrops, points and community incentives sets out how each mechanism shapes behaviour.

A holder with nothing to do is a seller waiting for a price. A holder with a job has a reason to stay that is not the chart.

Give holders a job

The jobs that work are real work, not engagement theatre:

  • Test new markets or features before they go live, with feedback visible and acted on.
  • Curate listings, parameters or content where judgment matters and you cannot automate it.
  • Govern decisions that have consequences, not polls about logo colours.
  • Refer people they are willing to vouch for, with their name on the referral.

Governance needs particular care, because token voting concentrates fast. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap found only about 5% of tokens were cast on a typical proposal and the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote.

Our piece on first customers as design partners described the first ten customers as design partners. Holders with a job are the same idea at a hundred people. Treat their output as product input, and say so publicly when it ships.

The first hundred in crypto, and the only metric

The first hundred argued that the first hundred people are the whole company for a while. In crypto, the trap is picking them by wallet balance. The first hundred you want are daily DeFi users: people who already move capital across protocols most days, understand the risks without being told, and will say plainly when something is wrong. Find them in governance forums, support channels and among people who read audit reports. Recruit them by hand and give them direct access to the team.

The only community metric worth trusting is retention measured after the money stops. Define it before you start. Pick the action that means someone is using the product, not visiting it. Run incentives for a set period. Then stop, and count how many people keep doing that action in the following weeks. That number is your community. Everything else is a cost of acquiring it.

Keep that record on systems you own: a member list, a contribution log, an email address or a wallet you can reach without a third party. Stop reporting reach made the general case. In crypto, start reporting who is still here.

lowob takeaways

  • Cost the airdrop. Plan it as an acquisition cost with an expected loss rate, not as a conversion.
  • Reward persistence. Weight allocation to repeated usage over time, and build sybil filters before the snapshot.
  • Assign a job. Holders who test, curate, govern or refer have a reason to stay that is not the price.
  • Count after the money stops. Retained usage after incentives end is the community; the rest is acquisition cost.

Common questions

How do you keep crypto users after an airdrop?

Design for the fraction who stay. Allocate for repeated usage over time, give holders a real job, keep their record on channels you own and measure who keeps using the product after incentives stop.

What percentage of airdrop recipients sell their tokens?

It varies by programme, but it is usually high. Dune data showed 93% of Uniswap airdrop recipients had sold all their UNI after two years, and one academic study found up to 66% of tokens in some airdrops were sold quickly.

Are airdrop farmers a problem?

Farmers are rational actors doing what the programme paid for. The mistake is counting them as users rather than planning the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected loss rate.

How should sybil filtering work for a token distribution?

Build it as a product feature before the snapshot, publish the rules in advance, apply them without exception, and keep an appeals channel that a human reads.

  • Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems, arXiv, revised July 2025. Academic preprint; nine airdrops, on-chain data to October 2024; exchange flows are a proxy for selling.
  • Dune, The Uniswap Airdrop: Lessons for the Industry, late 2022. Community analysis on Dune's analytics platform; data to September 2022; one airdrop.
  • Keyrock, Airdrops in the Barren Desert, 25 September 2024. Research by a crypto market maker; 62 airdrops in 2024; price performance, not user retention.
  • The Block, Kaito token plummets after X revises API policies to ban InfoFi crypto projects, 15 January 2026. News report; intraday price data.
  • Falk, Pathan, Rigas and Tsoukalas, Blockchain Governance: An Empirical Analysis of User Engagement on DAOs, arXiv, 15 July 2024. Preprint; four DeFi protocols to December 2022.

Next move

Before your next distribution, write down the action that means someone is really using the product and the date incentives will stop. Thirty days after that date, count who is still doing it and report that number alongside the claim rate.
